These likely primary magnetizations, in conjunction with data from the literature, give an overall mean Late Oligocene±Middle Miocene paleomagnetic pole which shows a large and significant counterclockwise rotation of . 528 "f88 with respect to the Africa reference paleopoles or a similar amount of rotation with respect to the coeval .Europe reference paleopole . This paper evaluates the possibility of large- scale vertical axis rotation of Bare Mountain re- lated to Basin and Range extension and the Walker Lane transtensional deformation using a detailed and systematic study of the paleomag- netism of Bare Mountain, Nevada. Specifically, paleomagnetic results from 12 Oligocene(?) and Miocene mafic and silicic porphyry dikes and 20 sites collected in the carbonate rocks of the Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation at Bare Mountain are presented. These results are also examined within the context of the Walker Lane and Basin and Range tectonics by comparing them to paleomagnetic directions from 13 addi- tional sites collected in the lower Paleozoic car- bonate rocks exposed

Demagnetization experiments revealed two distinct remanence components in the Ordovician carbonate rocks: (1) a dual polarity Permian-Triassic magnetization carried by magnetite that was acquired after Paleozoic or Mesozoic folding but prior to Tertiary tilting; and (2) a dual po- larity Miocene magnetization carried by hematite that was acquired after folding and tilting. The Tertiary dikes also contain a dual polarity magnetization carried by magnetite that can be interpreted either as a primary thermoremanent magnetization or a sec- ondary chemical remanent magnetization ac- quired shortly after dike intrusion. Overall, mean directions for all three magnetizations roughly coincide with corresponding refer- ence directions for Nevada. ozoic or Mesozoic folding but prior to Tertiary tilting; and (2) a dual po- larity Miocene magnetization carried by hematite that was acquired after folding and tilting. The Tertiary dikes also contain a dual polarity magnetization carried by magnetite that can be interpreted either as a primary thermoremanent magnetization or a sec- ondary chemical remanent magnetization ac- quired shortly after dike intrusion. Overall, mean directions for all three magnetizations roughly coincide with corresponding refer- ence directions for Nevada. The largest decli- nation discordance of 16° ± 7° (clockwise) comes from comparison of the Permian- Triassic magnetite magnetization to the Late Permian reference direction for Nevada. Thus, although structural and geothermal data, including zircon fission-track ages, indi- cate that northern Bare Mountain was tilted 20°–40° northeastward about a horizontal axis during early Tertiary time, we find no ev- idence for large-scale (i.e., >30°) vertical-axis rotation. ral Basin and Range extensional province of Wernicke (1992). Bare Mountain is part of the diffuse belt of deforma- tion known as the Walker Lane that consists of spatially segregated regions of east-west exten- sion between northwest-trending zones of dextral strike-slip or oblique-slip faulting (Stewart, 1988; Oldow et al., 1994). Deformation within the Walker Lane and central Basin and Range is manifested by kilometer-scale translation of up- per crustal blocks coupled with rotations about horizontal, steeply inclined, and vertical axes. Vertical-axis rotations of crustal blocks within the Walker Lane have been documented and quantified by paleomagnetic results. For exam- ple, paleomagnetic directions identified as Ceno- zoic and Permian-Triassic secondary magnetiza- tions in Paleozoic carbonate rocks and primary magnetizations in Cenozoic (mainly Miocene) clastic rocks and nonmarine limestones show as much as 100° of clockwise rotation associated with motion along the Las Vegas Valley shear (Gillett and Van Alstine, 1982; Nelson and Jones, 1987; Sonder et al., 1994). Significant clockwise rotations are also observed in the Black Moun- tains, presumably in response to similar right-lat- eral shear along the Death Valley–Furnace Creek fault zone (Holm et al., 1993), and in the Cotton- wood Mountain

resumably in response to west-northwest Basin and Range extension (Snow et al., 1993). Despite large rotations in many parts of the Walker Lane, paleomagnetic evidence for sig- nificant vertical-axis rotations in the region around Yucca Mountain and at Bare Mountain is equivocal. Primary magnetization directions from most of the middle Miocene volcanic rocks of the southwestern Nevada volcanic field are not systematically rotated (Hudson, 1992; Hudson et al., 1994), except within the southern reaches of Yucca Mountain (Rosenbaum et al., 1991) and in southwestern Crater Flat, just south of Bare Mountain (Hudson et al., 1996). Yet, preliminary paleomagnetic results from two Miocene dikes at Bare Mountain do not in- dicate any vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block (Zhang et al., 1993). Structural and sedimentological evidence for large-magnitude vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block is also equivocal. Bare Mountain is part of the diffuse belt of deforma- tion known as the Walker Lane that consists of spatially segregated regions of east-west exten- sion between northwest-trending zones of dextral strike-slip or oblique-slip faulting (Stewart, 1988; Oldow et al., 1994). Deformation within the Walker Lane and central Basin and Range is manifested by kilometer-scale translation of up- per crustal blocks coupled with rotations about horizontal, steeply inclined, and vertical axes. Vertical-axis rotations of crustal blocks within the Walker Lane have been documented and quantified by paleomagnetic results. For exam- ple, paleomagnetic directions identified as Ceno- zoic and Permian-Triassic secondary magnetiza- tions in Paleozoic carbonate rocks and primary magnetizations in Cenozoic (mainly Miocene) clastic rocks and nonmarine limestones show as much as 100° of clockwise rotation associated with motion along the Las Vegas Valley shear (Gillett and Van Alstine, 1982; Nelson and Jones, 1987; Sonder et al., 1994). Significant clockwise rotations are also observed in the Black Moun- tains, presumably in response to similar right-lat- eral shear along the Death Valley–Furnace Creek fault zone (Holm et al., 1993), and in the Cotton- wood Mountain

resumably in response to west-northwest Basin and Range extension (Snow et al., 1993). Despite large rotations in many parts of the Walker Lane, paleomagnetic evidence for sig- nificant vertical-axis rotations in the region around Yucca Mountain and at Bare Mountain is equivocal. Primary magnetization directions from most of the middle Miocene volcanic rocks of the southwestern Nevada volcanic field are not systematically rotated (Hudson, 1992; Hudson et al., 1994), except within the southern reaches of Yucca Mountain (Rosenbaum et al., 1991) and in southwestern Crater Flat, just south of Bare Mountain (Hudson et al., 1996). Yet, preliminary paleomagnetic results from two Miocene dikes at Bare Mountain do not in- dicate any vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block (Zhang et al., 1993). Structural and sedimentological evidence for large-magnitude vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block is also equivocal. Snow (1992; 1994), for example, envisioned the Pan- ama and Meiklejohn Peak thrusts exposed at Bare Mountain as rotated segments of an Early Per- mian, pre-Sonoma thrust system that is also ex- posed in the Cottonwood Range in northern Death Valley. Reconstruction of the thrust system predicts large-scale translation along a Cenozoic regional detachment and a 90° clockwise vertic

In this model, the Amargosa Desert fault system, which includes the Bare Mountain fault, has presumably accumulated more than 30 km of dextral displacement since the mid-Miocene with minimal vertical-axis rota- tion of the Bare Mountain block. This paper evaluates the possibility of large- scale vertical axis rotation of Bare Mountain re- lated to Basin and Range extension and the Walker Lane transtensional deformation using a detailed and systematic study of the paleomag- netism of Bare Mountain, Nevada. Specifically, paleomagnetic results from 12 Oligocene(?) and Miocene mafic and silicic porphyry dikes and 20 sites collected in the carbonate rocks of the Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation at Bare Mountain are presented. These results are also examined within the context of the Walker Lane and Basin and Range tectonics by comparing them to paleomagnetic directions from 13 addi- tional sites collected in the lower Paleozoic car- bonate rocks exposed in nearby ranges of the Yucca Mountain region, as well as previously published paleomagnetic results from other ranges in Nevada and Utah. Bare Mountain is part of the diffuse belt of deforma- tion known as the Walker Lane that consists of spatially segregated regions of east-west exten- sion between northwest-trending zones of dextral strike-slip or oblique-slip faulting (Stewart, 1988; Oldow et al., 1994). Deformation within the Walker Lane and central Basin and Range is manifested by kilometer-scale translation of up- per crustal blocks coupled with rotations about horizontal, steeply inclined, and vertical axes. Vertical-axis rotations of crustal blocks within the Walker Lane have been documented and quantified by paleomagnetic results. For exam- ple, paleomagnetic directions identified as Ceno- zoic and Permian-Triassic secondary magnetiza- tions in Paleozoic carbonate rocks and primary magnetizations in Cenozoic (mainly Miocene) clastic rocks and nonmarine limestones show as much as 100° of clockwise rotation associated with motion along the Las Vegas Valley shear (Gillett and Van Alstine, 1982; Nelson and Jones, 1987; Sonder et al., 1994). Significant clockwise rotations are also observed in the Black Moun- tains, presumably in response to similar right-lat- eral shear along the Death Valley–Furnace Creek fault zone (Holm et al., 1993), and in the Cotton- wood Mountain

resumably in response to west-northwest Basin and Range extension (Snow et al., 1993). Despite large rotations in many parts of the Walker Lane, paleomagnetic evidence for sig- nificant vertical-axis rotations in the region around Yucca Mountain and at Bare Mountain is equivocal. Primary magnetization directions from most of the middle Miocene volcanic rocks of the southwestern Nevada volcanic field are not systematically rotated (Hudson, 1992; Hudson et al., 1994), except within the southern reaches of Yucca Mountain (Rosenbaum et al., 1991) and in southwestern Crater Flat, just south of Bare Mountain (Hudson et al., 1996). Yet, preliminary paleomagnetic results from two Miocene dikes at Bare Mountain do not in- dicate any vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block (Zhang et al., 1993). Structural and sedimentological evidence for large-magnitude vertical-axis rotations of the Bare Mountain block is also equivocal. Snow (1992; 1994), for example, envisioned the Pan- ama and Meiklejohn Peak thrusts exposed at Bare Mountain as rotated segments of an Early Per- mian, pre-Sonoma thrust system that is also ex- posed in the Cottonwood Range in northern Death Valley. Reconstruction of the thrust system predicts large-scale translation along a Cenozoic regional detachment and a 90° clockwise vertic

In this model, the Amargosa Desert fault system, which includes the Bare Mountain fault, has presumably accumulated more than 30 km of dextral displacement since the mid-Miocene with minimal vertical-axis rota- tion of the Bare Mountain block. This paper evaluates the possibility of large- scale vertical axis rotation of Bare Mountain re- lated to Basin and Range extension and the Walker Lane transtensional deformation using a detailed and systematic study of the paleomag- netism of Bare Mountain, Nevada. Specifically, paleomagnetic results from 12 Oligocene(?) and Miocene mafic and silicic porphyry dikes and 20 sites collected in the carbonate rocks of the Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation at Bare Mountain are presented. These results are also examined within the context of the Walker Lane and Basin and Range tectonics by comparing them to paleomagnetic directions from 13 addi- tional sites collected in the lower Paleozoic car- bonate rocks exposed in nearby ranges of the Yucca Mountain region, as well as previously published paleomagnetic results from other ranges in Nevada and Utah. Demagnetization experiments revealed two distinct remanence components in the Ordovician carbonate rocks: (1) a dual polarity Permian-Triassic magnetization carried by magnetite that was acquired after Paleozoic or Mesozoic folding but prior to Tertiary tilting; and (2) a dual po- larity Miocene magnetization carried by hematite that was acquired after folding and tilting. The Tertiary dikes also contain a dual polarity magnetization carried by magnetite that can be interpreted either as a primary thermoremanent magnetization or a sec- ondary chemical remanent magnetization ac- quired shortly after dike intrusion. ozoic or Mesozoic folding but prior to Tertiary tilting; and (2) a dual po- larity Miocene magnetization carried by hematite that was acquired after folding and tilting. The Tertiary dikes also contain a dual polarity magnetization carried by magnetite that can be interpreted either as a primary thermoremanent magnetization or a sec- ondary chemical remanent magnetization ac- quired shortly after dike intrusion. Overall, mean directions for all three magnetizations roughly coincide with corresponding refer- ence directions for Nevada. The largest decli- nation discordance of 16° ± 7° (clockwise) comes from comparison of the Permian- Triassic magnetite magnetization to the Late Permian reference direction for Nevada. Thus, although structural and geothermal data, including zircon fission-track ages, indi- cate that northern Bare Mountain was tilted 20°–40° northeastward about a horizontal axis during early Tertiary time, we find no ev- idence for large-scale (i.e., >30°) vertical-axis rotation. On the basis of these results, we sug- gest that Bare Mountain forms an autochtho- nous or parautochthonous footwall within the Basin and Range and Walker Lane, in a re- gion where many of the surrounding upper crustal rocks are detached and significantly rotated about vertical and steeply inclined

Introduction Three contrasting models for genesis of Jurassic ophiolitic rocks in the western Coast Ranges of California have recently been discussed by Dickinson et al. [1996]. Although these models share broad similarities within a plate tectonic framework, each hypothesis has distinct implications for development of the continental margin. Points of origin outlined for the Coast Range ophiolite are (1) backarc spreading behind an east facing intraoceanic subruction zone, (2) mid-ocean spreading at equatorial paleolatitudes, and (3) spreading within the forearc region due to transtensional de- formation. While the first and third hypotheses require little or no latitudinal displacements relative to the North American craton, the second implies significant northward translation from the palcoequator. Introduction Three contrasting models for genesis of Jurassic ophiolitic rocks in the western Coast Ranges of California have recently been discussed by Dickinson et al. [1996]. Although these models share broad similarities within a plate tectonic framework, each hypothesis has distinct implications for development of the continental margin. Points of origin outlined for the Coast Range ophiolite are (1) backarc spreading behind an east facing intraoceanic subruction zone, (2) mid-ocean spreading at equatorial paleolatitudes, and (3) spreading within the forearc region due to transtensional de- formation. We present a magnetostratigraphic study of three pelagic limestone sections (Gamsstein, Mendlingbach and Mayerling) from the eastern part of the Northern Calcareous Alps. Together these sections, which contain a rich conodont fauna, yield a sedimentary record encompassing the uppermost Anisian, the Ladinian and the Lower Carnian. Thermal demagnetization and isothermal remanent magnetization experiments indicate that the magnetization is essentially carried by a mineral of the magnetite family. The discordance between the two groups is striking, given that recent U-Pb dating of rocks from the Belt Supergroup demonstrates that most of the rocks from which the two groups of poles are derived are approximately coeval [Aleinikoff et al., 1996]. Introduction Recent estimates of Colorado Plateau (CP) rotation based on direct paleomagnetic pole comparisons have focused on a relatively large data set from Upper Triassic strata, a time interval during which apparent polar wander (APW) of North America has been interpreted to be slow to negligible [Kent and Witte, 1993; Kent and Olsen, 1997]. Paleomagnetic data for the Newark Supergroup, on which the hypothesis of small to negligible APW is based, include the mid to upper Camian Stockton and Lockatong formations, the lower to upper Norian Passaic Formation, and overlying Hettangian basalts and sedimentary rocks (an interval from -228 to 205 Ma). Other paleomagnetic data, however, have been interpreted to indicate that Late Triassic APW of North America is significant. Kodama et al. [1994] showed evidence of Late Triassic APW from Mesozoic rocks of noaheast

for strata of unquestionably different age. A few million years would not affect previous estimates of large CP rotation if Late Triassic APW was indeed negligible, but the age difference between cratonic and CP poles is sufficient to bias a rotation estimate if APW was rapid. The new pole for the upper Carnian Bluewater Creek Formation reported here provides a datum of crucial importance to (1) test the hypothesis of a Late Triassic stand still in the North American APW path and (2) improve estimates of CP rotation based on Triassic results. This manuscript focuses on the first issue; regardless of the magnitude of CP rotation, paleopoles from rocks on and off the plateau should record similar amounts of APW. From the determination of two new pole positions and teevaluation of previously published data, we suggest that APW was neither small nor slow during the Late Triassic. This is important not only for understanding the kinematics of deformation along the western margin of North America but also in determining the motion of the North American craton during the Mesozoic. The preservation of recognizable bedding in these slump blocks allowed us to use these samples in a modified conglomerate test. Following sample preparation, all specimens were stored and analyzed in a magnetically shielded room with background field intensity < 200 nT. NRM was measured with a three-axis cryogenic magnetometer (2G model 755R). Thermal demagne- tizations at 14 to 18 steps up to 680øC were accomplished using furnaces with magnetic field intensity less than 10 nT in the sample region. Results of thermal demagnetization were analyzed by principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980], and site-mean directions were determined using the statistical methods of Fisher [1953]. Samples were oriented using both magnetic compass and solar compass. No significant deviations were noted between these orientation methods. An additional 14 samples were taken from slumped blocks at one particular level of the Vilavila Formation. The preservation of recognizable bedding in these slump blocks allowed us to use these samples in a modified conglomerate test. Following sample preparation, all specimens were stored and analyzed in a magnetically shielded room with background field intensity < 200 nT. NRM was measured with a three-axis cryogenic magnetometer (2G model 755R). Thermal demagne- tizations at 14 to 18 steps up to 680øC were accomplished using furnaces with magnetic field intensity less than 10 nT in the sample region. Results of thermal demagnetization were analyzed by principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980], and site-mean directions were determined using the statistical methods of Fisher [1953]. Accordingly, assignment of percent folding at the time of remagnetization of Paleozoic strata at Villamontes lacks precision (Figure 8). This paper reports the paleomagnetic and geochronological analysis of a suite of samples from a basaltic fault-related scarp of Pliocene age in the central part of the Afar depression (Ethiopia). Paleomagnetic work uncovers a clear characteristic remanent magnetization carried by (titano-) magnetites, with high unblocking temperatures, close to the Curie temperature of pure magnetite. The characteristic direction, based on 27 non transitional flows, is D=8.1 o, I= 10.1 o (5=4.1 o). This is consistent with earlier determinations of the clockwise tectonic rotation, due to rift propagation and overlap, of the block to which the section belongs. Magnetic stratigraphy consists of a succession from bottom to top of 16 reversed, 7 normal, and 4 reversed flows. One flow at the upper normal to reverse transition demonstrates complex behavior upon thermal and alternating field (AF) demagnetization, which is due to remagnetization by the overlying flow. Mid-Cretaceous volcanic rocks con- sist of andesitic feldspar porphyry flows and tuffs of the Mount Nansen Group. Felsic volcanic rocks deposited across south- central Yukon between 84 and 78 Ma, including pyroclastic flows and flow-banded rhyolite, are included in the Windy–Table Suite (Mihalynuk et al. 1992; Hart 1995). Vo- luminous sequences of subaerial volcanic rocks deposited across central Yukon between 72 and 69 Ma, including exten- sive flood basalts, are included in the Carmacks Group (Tem- pelman-Kluit 1974; Grond et al. 1984). Paleomagnetic field and laboratory procedures Drill cores (typically six) or hand samples (three) were col- lected at each site and oriented using both magnetic and solar compasses. The solar and magnetic bearings agreed within 2° except where the rocks had been hit by lightning and were, as a consequence, strongly magnetic. Solar bearings were used for these rocks. Specimens were measured in the laboratory using a robotized Schonstedt DSM1 fluxgate magnetometer or a Geofyzika JR5A spinner magnetometer. Specimens were de- magnetized using five to 10 demagnetization steps, using a Schonstedt TSD-1 therm

Three sites (W61–W63) were collected from isolated outcrops along the Klondike Highway north of Carmacks. The cores from the Carmacks Agate Quarry (site W61) are relatively unaltered, finely crystalline basalt with 0.2–5 cm quartz-filled amygdules. It appears, therefore, that, like the Mandanna Member, the Nordenskiöld Formation at this locality was totally overprinted, after tilting, at the time of extrusion of the Carmacks Group. The interpretation for the Cinnamon Bun Row locality re- manence is less straightforward. The mean direction before tectonic correction is nearly vertical, which implies magneti- zation at the north pole. But after tectonic correction, the di- rection is shallow even compared with the Carmacks remanence. There are at least three ways this result can be interpreted: (i) the remanence could be primary, but it is shal- low compared with other Jurassic paleomagnetic data obtained in the southern Intermontane Belt (e.g., Monger and Irving 1980); (ii) the remanence could be a predeformational Creta- ceous overprint, implying an approximately 60° clockwise vertical axis rotation; and (iii) the remanence could be a post- deformational Cretaceous overprint followed by a further tilt of 20° down towards 347°NNW. Tilts of this magnitude have been observed in the Carmacks Formation elsewhere and so it is not unreasonable to invoke a late tilt. This explains the dis- crepancy between the locality mean direction of Cinnamon Bun Row (tilted after being overprinted during extrusion of the Carmacks Group) and that of Atlin Lake (not tilted after over- printing), and we favour this interpretation. Paleomagnetic analyses using alternating field and thermal step demagnetization methods were run on 229 specimens from 24 sites in and adjacent to the pluton. Its characteristic remanent magnetization direction (ChRM) is shown from thermal demagnetization and saturation isothermal remanence analyses to reside mostly in single domain to multidomain magnetite, commonly with high unblocking temperatures near the 585°C Curie temperature, but sometimes in pyrrhotite. From stratigraphic data Kolata and Nelson (1991) estimate uplift at between 2.4 and 4.6 km. Similarly, Leach et al. (1994) set uplift at between 2.1 and 3.7 km using conodont alteration index val- ues. Arguing that some time must be left for erosion of the uplift prior to overlying Late Cretaceous sedi- mentation, Kolata and Nelson (1991, fig. 1) suggest an end to uplift in mid-Jurassic time. This uplift must be assumed to have been in response to large intra- plate tectonic forces and to have caused a major pe- riod of reactivation on the fluorspar district faults. The speculation is, therefore, that the Rosiclare event coincides with the Mesozoic uplift event with concomitant fault reactivation and northeasterly fluid flow in the Reelfoot-Wabash rift zone. Conclusions The results of this paleomagnetic study of fluorspar ores and their host rocks in the Illinois-Kentucky dis- trict lead to the following conclusions: 1. Mississippian limestones from some 200 km to the northeast near Louisville, which are stratigraphi- cally equivalent to the host rocks, retain an A charac- teristic RM component. SYMONS Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario, Canada N9B 3P44 Abstract The Illinois-Kentucky fluorspar district has yielded most of the United States fluorite pro- duction. The fluorspar ore occurs as epigenetic replacement deposits in Mississippian lime- stone and as vein deposits. Palcomagnetic analysis was done on 324 specimens from 33 sites in fluorspar ore and in host limestones and cap-rock sandstones both adjacent to and remote from ore using alternating field and thermal step demagnetization. Saturation isothermal remanence methods were used to identify magnetization carriers in typical specimens and mineral crystals. An A characteristic remanent magnetization (RM) component was found outside the district in stratigraphically equivalent limestones that record a Pennsylvanian Kiaman remagnetization, and a C characteristic RM was found in surface weathered speci- mens that records the Recent earth's magnetic field. At 28 sites in ore and nearby host rocks a B characteristic RM was found that gives a Late Jurassic pole position of 152.4 ø E, 78.0 ø N (dp = 3.0 ø, dm = 4.4ø). The object of this study was to use palcomagnetic methods to date the ore and, thereby, to constrain geologic models for genesis of the fluor- spar ore. (1989) have recently summarized the extensive geologic literature of the district. Genevieve Lime- stone beds beneath the Rosiclare Sandstone Member, and Bethel ore in limestones of the uppermost beds of the Downeys Bluff Member of the Renault Forma- tion beneath the Bethel Sandstone Member (Baxter et al., 1992). The mantos range up to 3 km in length, 60 m in width, and 6 m in thickness; they occur next to major northeast-trending faults beneath cap-rock sandstones. The vein deposits are predominantly in the northeast-trending faults and mainly within the walls of the middle Mississippian strata. However, trace amounts of fluorite are found in faults cutting lower Pennsylvanian rocks. The vein deposits range up to about 250 m vertically and horizontally and up to 14 m in width. From stratigraphic data Kolata and Nelson (1991) estimate uplift at between 2.4 and 4.6 km. Similarly, Leach et al. (1994) set uplift at between 2.1 and 3.7 km using conodont alteration index val- ues. Arguing that some time must be left for erosion of the uplift prior to overlying Late Cretaceous sedi- mentation, Kolata and Nelson (1991, fig. 1) suggest an end to uplift in mid-Jurassic time. This uplift must be assumed to have been in response to large intra- plate tectonic forces and to have caused a major pe- riod of reactivation on the fluorspar district faults. The speculation is, therefore, that the Rosiclare event coincides with the Mesozoic uplift event with concomitant fault reactivation and northeasterly fluid flow in the Reelfoot-Wabash rift zone. Some support comes from Bethke et al. An obvious speculation is that hot brines moving northeasterly from deep in the Reelfoot rift on Pas- cola arch uplift (Goldhaber et al., 1992b; Leach et al., 1994) may have met and mixed with lower tem- perature brines at the juncture with the crosscutting Ste. Genevieve-Rough Creek fault zone. Fourth, it is not realistic to hypothesize that the fluorspar de- posits were emplaced at 272 Ma only to have their characteristic RM reset by heating in the Late Juras- sic. The rank of the Pennsylvanian coal beds in the area indicates only 1,300 m of burial (Schwalb, 1982) and the dominant fluid inclusion temperatures of 140 ø to 153øC also limit postemplacement heating to less than about 100øC. Such temperatures are far too low to have reset a single domain to pseudosingle domain remanence in magnetite with unblocking tem- peratures

ociated with any known igneous intrusions. Sixth, this study may add another high-latitude Jurassic pole for eastern North America (Van Fossen and Kent, 1990), although it should not be used for appar- ent polar wander path construction until confirmed by another dating method. Conclusions The results of this paleomagnetic study of fluorspar ores and their host rocks in the Illinois-Kentucky dis- trict lead to the following conclusions: 1. Mississippian limestones from some 200 km to the northeast near Louisville, which are stratigraphi- cally equivalent to the host rocks, retain an A charac- teristic RM component. It resides in single domain to pseudosingle domain magnetite and has a reversed polarization. A gives a mid-Pennsylvanian pole posi- tion that is typical of Kiaman remagnetization of older Paleozoic limestones throughout much of the U. S. midcontinent. 2. During the Late Jurassic, the district's lime- stone host rocks and sandstone cap rocks, which prob- ably carried a Kiaman remanence, were remagne- tized to carry the B characteristic RM. Coincidentally the fluorspar ore was emplaced with the B character- istic RM. These results show that the hydrothermal dolomite sheets and associated Mississippi Valley-type deposits were formed with a primary chemical characteristic remanent mag- netization during Late Cretaceous Laramide uplift and defor- mation. It follows, therefore, that Laramide structures will provide one control for Mississippi Valley-type mineralization in the southern Rocky Mountains. The results also show that the Cambrian dolostone host rocks were either limestones which were dolomitized to acquire a primary remanence or dolostones which were recrystallized to acquire a reset sec- ondary remanence during the Late Cretaceous. Beview of the evidence to date leads to the conclusion that the most significant fluid flow event in the western Canada sedimentary basin occurred in response to the Lara- mide orogeny. The stratigraphic, structural, palcomagnetic, fission track, hydrogeologic modeling, and most other cited evidence supports this statement. he timing of the fluid flow event(s) eausing dolomitization in the western Canada sedimentary ba- sin has been debated with some researchers favoring a Creta- eeous-Paleoeene flow related to the Laramide orogeny (e.g., Garven, 1985; Qing and Mountjoy, 1992) and others arguing for an earlier age, usually mid to late Paleozoie, from a pre- Laramide flow (e.g., Nesbitt and Muehlenbaehs, 1991; Yao and Demieeo, 1995). Oliver (1986, 1992) noted the relationship on a continental scale between orogenesis and the spots and stains of the related fluid flows that include regional dolomitization, transport of petroleum into reservoirs, and the formation of Mississippi Valley-type zinc-lead-barite deposits. These fea- tures are difficult to date radiometrically because they com- monly lack suitable minerals in sufficient concentrations. How- ever, palcomagnetic methods have been used to date nine major Mississippi Valley-type deposits in North America and shown in every ease that they are coeval with orogenesis in the surrounding or adjacent orogen (Symons et al., 1996). They have been cut by the Early Proterozoic Hearst diabase dikes, which trend north-south and dip nearly vertically (Emst and Halls 1984). The complex is nearly circular, with a diameter of about 5.5 km. It comprises dominantly massive, coarse-grained leucocratic nepheline syenite that forms both the core and the periphery. In between are arcuate bands and partial rings of foliated malignite - ijolite that dip at 40° - 65 towards the centre. Within these bands on the north side is a small zone of calcic carbonatite. On the west side of these bands is an inte- rior zone of iiolite breccia, with abundant magnetite, and on the north side is an exterior zone of ijolite breccia called the Portage Lake Complex. The syenite and mafic alkalic rocks are cut in turn by carbonatite veins with pyrochlore that carry the niobium values, by the apatite - magnetite veins, and finally by occasional lamprophyre dikes that are not exposed. The contacts of the complex are apparently vertical, and the adjacent wall rocks are fenitized. There is no petrologic evi- dence of postintrusive metamorphism of the complex. Recently, Halls and Pesonen (1982) and Palmer and Davis (1987) evalu- ated the paleomagnetic and radiometric data base for the Logan Loop, and the Lackner pole falls at about 1108 f 10 Ma on it (Fig. 7). This paleomagnetic age agrees well with the K- Ar age of 1086 f 60 Ma and the pooled Rb - Sr isochron age of 1092 f 21 Ma. It is, however, a normal pole in a reversed- polarity part of the APWP. The simplest explanation is that the complex records a brief normal-polarity interval in a dorni- nantly reversed portion of the path. Another explanation could be that the complex is actually about 1090 Ma old, in which case its original pole position would be close to MPl (Fig. 7). If true, then the complex would have to have been tilted about 30°W about a horizontal north-northeast axis to give its present pole. Yet another possibility is that the pole reflects a postintrusive metamorphic event. This seems untenable for several reasons. First, the rocks show no evidence of postintrusive metamor- phism (Sage 1983). Second, excluding perhaps the nearly con- temporaneous Nemegosenda Complex, there are no known younger intrusions in the area. Third, the step-demagnetization I data show no evidence of an underlying older remanence com- ponent. Fourth, the APWP is not known to pass through the Lackner Lake position at any subsequent time (Irving 1979). Thus the best and preferred explanation is that the Lackner pole is concordant and reflects a primary untilted remanence direction. ferous limestone and chert clasts from the Cache Creek Terrane into Middle to Late Jurassic conglomerates of the Bowser Basin. Similarly, the Early Jurassic Inkdin Formation of the Cache Creek Terrane contains detritus believed to be derived from the Quesnellia terrane (Monger et al. 1991). Thus, by Middle Jurassic, the Stikinia, Quesnellia, and Cache Greek terranes were at least loosely amalgamated and located next to the craton. Previous paleomagnetic studies suggest that the terranes underlying the Insular Belt (Fig. 2) may have collided with those of the Intermontane Belt by mid-Cretaceous to Late Cretaceous time to create a fairly coherent assemblage located some 1000-2880 km south of its present position (Irving and Wynne 1991 ; Irving et al. 1996), with the Coast Plutonic Complex marking the intervening suture (Monger et al. 1982). Subsequently, this assemblage of terranes moved north-northwesterly in panels on dominantly dextral faults beside the North American craton, reaching their present position in the Late Eocene ( - 45 Ma) (Irving et ad. 1996). Paleomagnetic data for Eocene (52 -44 Ma) rocks throughout the Canadian Cordillera, except for the Queen Charlotte Islands (Irving and Wynne 1991), show that the Cordilleran terranes have not moved signif

Aeromagnetic surveys indi- cate its eastern contact dips steeply, and drilling indicates a steep to locally overhanging contact on the west and an out- ward shallow-dipping contact on its north and south sides (Morrison 1981; Hart and Pelletier 1989). Contact attitudes indicate that the pluton has not been tilted, assuming vertical emplacement. Pendants of host rock are numerous dong the northern, western, and southern margins, but are not observed along the eastern margin because of lower erosional levels and the presence of the overburden. Based on thin-section analyses and field observations for all paleomagnetic sites and elsewhere, the rock types include diorite, quartz diorite, quartz monzo- diorite, tonalite, and granodiorite. Most have medium- to coarse-grained plagioclase in a fine- to medium-grained matrix of quartz and mafic minerals (Hart and Radloff 1990). The major minerals are plagioclase, quartz, hornblende, and biotite. Minor and accessory minerals include magnetite, potassium feldspar, titanite, and apatite. Larger hornblende crystals typically have clinopyroxene cores. The anorthite content of plagioclase ranges from Anl9 to An34 (average Anz5), and some albite may be present. Visible potassium feldspar crystals are rare, but perthite is common. The pluton is variably altered, as the presence of chlorite, epidote, and carbonate suggests. Zones of hydrothermal alteration in the northern part of the pluton are probably related to adjacent copper -gold skarn deposits in that region (Morrison 198 1 ; Hart and Pelletier 1989 ; Hart and Radloff 1990; Hart 1995). It is in fault contact on the east with the Cache Creek Terrane, but the origind nature of its western contact has been masked by Cretaceous and Tertiary plutonism and metamorphism of the Coast Plutonic Complex. The upper Paleozoic and Triassic rocks of Stikinia are thought to reflect an island-arc setting, with its 4QO h long belt of Mississippian and Permian lirne- stones recording an interval when the terrane was a stable block (Gabrielse et al. 1991b). During the Middle Jurassic, the Cache Creek Terrane was thrust over the northern and eastern margins of Stikinia, depositing diagnostic fossili- ferous limestone and chert clasts from the Cache Creek Terrane into Middle to Late Jurassic conglomerates of the Bowser Basin. Similarly, the Early Jurassic Inkdin Formation of the Cache Creek Terrane contains detritus believed to be derived from the Quesnellia terrane (Monger et al. 1991). Thus, by Middle Jurassic, the Stikinia, Quesnellia, and Cache Greek terranes were at least loosely amalgamated and located next to the craton. Previous paleomagnetic studies suggest that the terranes underlying the Insular Belt (Fig. 2) may have collided with those of the Intermontane Belt by mid-Cretaceous to Late Cretaceous time to create a fairly coherent as

ic Complex marking the intervening suture (Monger et al. 1982). Subsequently, this assemblage of terranes moved north-northwesterly in panels on dominantly dextral faults beside the North American craton, reaching their present position in the Late Eocene ( - 45 Ma) (Irving et ad. 1996). Paleomagnetic data for Eocene (52 -44 Ma) rocks throughout the Canadian Cordillera, except for the Queen Charlotte Islands (Irving and Wynne 1991), show that the Cordilleran terranes have not moved significantly with respect to the North American craton since then. Local The ovate Whitehorse Pluton is exposed over 160 h2 (Fig. 3). It intrudes two members of the Late Triassic Lewes River Group. The Hancock Member comprises up to 6W m of limestones and minor siltstones, and the overlying Man- danna Member comprises up to several hundred metres of crystal-rich, volcanogenic lithic greywacke and shale with minor red, bioturbated siltstone and pebble conglomerate (Hart and Radloff 199Q). The southern part of the Whitehorse Pluton is intruded by a few narrow vertical diabase dikes of uncertain age. The main conclusions of this work are that: (1) a Phanerozoic MVT mineralization event can be dated to within 4- 15 Ma using palaeomagnetism and it is usually a more reliable method than any radiometric technique at pre- sent; (2) every MVT event studied to date is coeval with a major orogenic event in the sur- rounding or adjacent orogen, supporting Oliver's (1986, 1992) assertion that MVT deposits are formed by fluid flow from an orogen; (3) host rock dolomitization may precede the mineraliza- tion event by a few million or tens of millions years (Lewchuk & Symons 1995); (4) the epige- netic mineralizing event itself may occur within a few milli

An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. Within the Thompson Belt the Molson dikes were deformed and metamorphosed during the Trans-Hudson Orogen. The dikes southeast of the belt, however, generally escaped this event. In the lower-grade terrain of the Superior Province, deuteric alteration of olivine to magnetite and serpentine occurs and varying degrees of crystal fractionation features are developed [Ermanovics and Fahrig, 1975]. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. Our principal objectives are to document differences in remanent magnetiz- ation within the Molson swarm that might define a multi- intrusive history and to interpret these data in terms of tectonic setting and their significance in the development of the Trans-Hudson Orogen. Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. Samples were mostly field drilled at Molson, Landing, Pikwitonei, Paint, Cauchon, and Witchai Lakes and block sampled elsewhere. Sun and magnetic compasses were used for each sample orientation. Both types of arguments are reexamined here. Using a new model of the Atlantic Ocean evolution described elsewhere, it is shown that the reconstructions of the positions of Africa relative to North America before the Atlantic opening, and at the times of magnetic anomalies M22 and J, do not imply a major motion of Morocco independent of Africa during these periods of time. The corresponding geomagnetic paleopoles have been recomputed from sample sites located on both "mobile" Morocco and "stable" Africa. The results indicate that the virtual geomagnetic pole of "mobile" Morocco for the Liassic falls within the 95% confidence cone of "stable" Africa. Paleomagnetic and radiometric data confirm the existence of two phases of igneous activity in the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic history of eastern Egypt. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N 101,5”E, A 95 = 27.8 (3 sites). The wide scatter is inter- preted as reflecting secular variation. The chronological and chemical data are used with studies of sedimentary forma- tions coeval with the igneous rocks to apply a general model of conti

asin col- lapse, and to transport of sediment towards the axial valley. Approximately 50 m.y. after the initial uplift, continental separation accompanied by tholei- itic volcanism begins. This takes no account of the subsequent spreading behaviour, that is, it is independent of the two spreading stages, proposed and discussed by Girdler and Styles (1976), Davidson and Rex (1980) and Richardson and Harrison (1976). The first, the trachytic (boston- itic) dikes, sills and plugs (B sites) intrude into the sediments of the Ham- mamet Formation and surrounding metamorphic rocks of the basement complex in the region southwest of Quseir (Fig. 1). Several of these units have been affected by uranium mineralization and these have been studied in detail by Hussein and El Kassas (1971, 1972). In the field the rocks usually form prominent relief and are recognizable by their light colored fine-grained character. 171 The rocks are composed predominantly of alkali feldspar and subordinate quartz, ferromagnesian minerals, zircon and apatite. As indicated earlier there are two phases of igneous activity, the first being volumetrically much more extensive than the second. The opening of the earlier phase was marked by the extrusion of alkaline basalts of which the Wadi Natash lavas are the best known (El Shazly and Krs, 1973), although slightly older lavas are reported from the. Wadi Amba in the northern Eastern Desert. The paleopole position of the lavas is indis- tinguishable from those obtained from the intrusions reported here. The radiometric age dates and the meagre fauna from the basal Nubian Sandstone Formation (Ward and McDonald, 1979) are consistent with a late Cretaceous age for the igneous units. The paleopole positions compare closely with those from other African rocks of similar age, on the assumption of zero relative motion between the Nubian and other African plates (Fig. 11). Paleomagnetic and radiometric data confirm the existence of two phases of igneous activity in the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic history of eastern Egypt. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N 101,5”E, A 95 = 27.8 (3 sites). The wide scatter is inter- preted as reflecting secular variation. The chronological and chemical data are used with studies of sedimentary forma- tions coeval with the igneous rocks to apply a general model of continental rifting to the northern Red Sea. The earlier, alkaline phase of igneous activity is related to regional up- lift while the second, tholeiitic phase is associated with widening of the rift valley. I. INTRODUCTION Scattered throughout the Eastern Desert of Egypt and at certain localities in the Western Desert are outcrops of igneous rocks which postdate the late Precambrian to early Phanerozoic Pan-African granites. With relatively few radiometric dates available, most workers have had to rely upon field criteria and composition to attempt a classification of the intrusions. Commonly these were grouped, from oldest to youngest, as acidic, intermediate, basic and alkaline intrusions. In the course of three field seasons we have collected samples from some 200 sites in the igneous rocks. The results to date suggest that the majority of these, including most of the acidic, intermediate and basic intrusions, are associated with the closing stages of the Pan-African event (Davies et al., 1980). The remaining, younger rocks include some which were emplaced since the mid to late Cretaceous and which constitute the subject of this paper. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion.

In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N 101,5”E, A 95 = 27.8 (3 sites). The wide scatter is inter- preted as reflecting secular variation. Thermomagnetic analysis Alkaline and basic-acid rock samples from all the studied units were analyzed with a thermomagnetic balance for the determination of Curie temperatures (T,) and the identification of magnetic minerals. section_candidates.excerpt: Itatiaia complex The Itatiaia alkaline complex (220 km’, Fig. 2) is located on the boundary between the states of Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. This intrudes into the Precambrian basement, which is represented by the Juiz de Fora metamorphic complex [7,17]. The Itati- aia massif is structurally linked to the SE Brazilian continental rift, which developed in an ENE to EW trending transcurrent system by the end of the BrasiI- iano (Pan African) Cycle and which was reactivated during the breakup of Gondwana [18]. The alkaline complex is composed of syenites, foyaites, pulask- ites, quartz syenites, magmatic breccias and alkaline granite [19]. The mean K-Ar age obtained on ten biotites from the Itatiaia rocks is 70.5 f 3.3 Ma [10,12]. 2.3. Passa Quatro complex The Passa Quatro alkaline complex (148 km*, Fig. 2) is close to the Itatiaia complex. It was emplaced into the Precambrian metamorphic com- plexes of Juiz de Fora, Paraiba do Sul and the Aqungui Group [7,17]. The main lithological types are alkali plutonic rocks (nepheline syenites) with minor phonolitic dykes. section_candidates.excerpt: Itatiaia complex The Itatiaia alkaline complex (220 km’, Fig. 2) is located on the boundary between the states of Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. This intrudes into the Precambrian basement, which is represented by the Juiz de Fora metamorphic complex [7,17]. The Itati- aia massif is structurally linked to the SE Brazilian continental rift, which developed in an ENE to EW trending transcurrent system by the end of the BrasiI- iano (Pan African) Cycle and which was reactivated during the breakup of Gondwana [18]. The alkaline complex is composed of syenites, foyaites, pulask- ites, quartz syenites, magmatic breccias and alkaline granite [19]. The mean K-Ar age obtained on ten biotites from the Itatiaia rocks is 70.5 f 3.3 Ma [10,12]. 2.3. Passa Quatro complex The Passa Quatro alkaline complex (148 km*, Fig. 2) is close to the Itatiaia complex. It was emplaced into the Precambrian metamorphic com- plexes of Juiz de Fora, Paraiba do Sul and the Aqungui Group [7,17]. The main lithological types are alkali plutonic rocks (nepheline syenites) with minor phonolitic dykes. section_candidates.excerpt: Itatiaia complex The Itatiaia alkaline complex (220 km’, Fig. 2) is located on the boundary between the states of Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. This intrudes into the Precambrian basement, which is represented by the Juiz de Fora metamorphic complex [7,17]. Paleomagnetic measurements for more than 4000 samples of lava and tuff indicate that nearly all of this >3500-m-thick sequence was laid down during one interval of normal magnetic polarity. Lavas of the lower third of this sequence are cut by the ore-bearing Noril'sk-I intrusion, which has an age of 251 Ma, identical to that of the Permian-Triassic boundary. Thus, the normal-polarity interval represented by this sequence is inferred to be the first of the Triassic Period. Eruption of this enormous volume of material in a relatively brief period coincident with the earth's greatest mass extinction requires that all aspects of Siberian flood-basalt volcanism be evaluated carefully as possibly contributing to that catastrophe. Stepwise thermal demagnetization of the subaerial mafic volcanics of the Ludlovian Fivemile Brook Formation of northwestern Maine reveals two ancient high-temperature, dual-polarity remanences. Fivemile Brook results AMS results indicate a low degree of anisotropy, indicating minimal probability of remanence deflec- tion. The ratios of bulk susceptibilities at 77 K to those at room temperature (293 K) indicate involve- ment of a paramagnetic mineral phase that is proba- bly chlorite. Moreover, the magnetic fabric observed in a number of Fivemile Brook sites is roughly cleavage parallel. Based on high unblocking temperatures it is in- ferred that both the c- and b-components are carried by hematite. In view of the extremely high tem- peratures required to thermally reset hematite grains (Pullaiah et al., 1976), both the c- and b-components are presumably chemical remanent magnetizations (CRMs) resulting from hematite replacement of orig- inal magnetite. Subaerial weathering may account for initial oxidation of the magnetite in these vol- canics; a later CRM may be associated with fluid circulation (Dorobek, 1989). The approximately antipodal directions are in- terpreted as a record of geomagnetic field rever- sals. The c-component clearly passes the common kappa reversal test. A tilt-corrected mean direction yields an inclination of 41 ° (~rl = 3.9 °, N = 4 sites) and the magnetization is interpreted as a near-primary magnetization acquired well before the end of Early Devonian deformation. An in situ mean direction (D = 165 °, 1 = 35 °, ~gs = 6 °, k = 65, N = 10 entries from 8 sites), is interpreted as a secondary overprint with a pole (22°S, 306°E) near the Early Carboniferous segment of the North American apparent polar wander path (APWP). The inclination-only fold test peaks at 50% unfolding with a mean inclination of -35 ° (~ = 8.5 °, n = 148). Synfolding acquisition of magnetization is Wenlockian, based on a negative conglomerate test at the base of the section and a positive conglomerate test at the top of the section. Clockwise streaking of site mean directions away from a predominantly northerly declination is consistent with post-middle W

ornquist sea, between Avalon and Baltica (Mac Niocaill and Smethurst, 1994). Upper Ordovician to Middle Devonian units in the northern Appalachians are generally brack- eted by Taconic and Acadian unconformities (Malo and Bourque, 1993). The Taconic orogenic pulse is associated with island arc accretion; the Silurian Salinic disturbance is associated with Avalonian col- lision and Iapetan closure; and the Acadian orogeny correlates with Devonian approach of Gondwana to Laurentia (van der Pluijm et al., 1993a; Van der Voo, 1993). The Silurian and Devonian rocks of the north- ern Appalachians form part of an overstep sequence deposited over the Central Mobile Belt. Silurian sed- imentary rocks form a southeast thickening wedge of shallow marine sedimentary rocks that grade from platformal carbonates in the northwest to central basinal shales and non-marine sandstones in the southeast (Keppie and Dostal, 1994). Silurian sed- iments were mainly derived from Laurentia to the northwest, whereas Lower Devonian flysch was derived from Avalon to the southeast. The Pis- cataquis and Tobique volcanic belts cross-cut the general structural trend of the northern Appalachi- ans (Fig. 1). Fivemile Brook results AMS results indicate a low degree of anisotropy, indicating minimal probability of remanence deflec- tion. The ratios of bulk susceptibilities at 77 K to those at room temperature (293 K) indicate involve- ment of a paramagnetic mineral phase that is proba- bly chlorite. Moreover, the magnetic fabric observed in a number of Fivemile Brook sites is roughly cleavage parallel. Based on high unblocking temperatures it is in- ferred that both the c- and b-components are carried by hematite. In view of the extremely high tem- peratures required to thermally reset hematite grains (Pullaiah et al., 1976), both the c- and b-components are presumably chemical remanent magnetizations (CRMs) resulting from hematite replacement of orig- inal magnetite. Subaerial weathering may account for initial oxidation of the magnetite in these vol- canics; a later CRM may be associated with fluid circulation (Dorobek, 1989). The approximately antipodal directions are in- terpreted as a record of geomagnetic field rever- sals. The c-component clearly passes the common kappa reversal test. ornquist sea, between Avalon and Baltica (Mac Niocaill and Smethurst, 1994). Upper Ordovician to Middle Devonian units in the northern Appalachians are generally brack- eted by Taconic and Acadian unconformities (Malo and Bourque, 1993). The Taconic orogenic pulse is associated with island arc accretion; the Silurian Salinic disturbance is associated with Avalonian col- lision and Iapetan closure; and the Acadian orogeny correlates with Devonian approach of Gondwana to Laurentia (van der Pluijm et al., 1993a; Van der Voo, 1993). The Silurian and Devonian rocks of the north- ern Appalachians form part of an overstep sequence deposited over the Central Mobile Belt. Silurian sed- imentary rocks form a southeast thickening wedge of shallow marine sedimentary rocks that grade from platformal carbonates in the northwest to central basinal shales and non-marine sandstones in the southeast (Keppie and Dostal, 1994). Silurian sed- iments were mainly derived from Laurentia to the northwest, whereas Lower Devonian flysch was derived from Avalon to the southeast. The Pis- cataquis and Tobique volcanic belts cross-cut the general structural trend of the northern Appalachi- ans (Fig. 1). In this paper, we report of a paleomagnetic study on the Early Cambrian to Middle Ordovician strata with de®nitively determined ages in the margin of the Ordos Basin of the NCB. Five paleomagnetic pole positions with ages ranging from the Early Cambrian to Middle Ordovician are established. ing the Early Cambrian to Middle Ordovician formations of the North China Block (NCB) to construct an apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the early Paleozoic for the NCB. Sampling areas are located in the Helanshan, Tongchuan-Hancheng and Yuncheng-Luliang regions along the margin of the Ordos Basin. Characteristic remanent magnetizations for ®ve periods between the Cambrian and Ordovician are isolated from 281 samples by careful demagnetization. Directions cluster around northwesterly direction with upward shallow inclination and its antipode after tilt correction. Reliability of these ®ve directions is ascertained through positive fold and reversal tests. The ®ve Cambrian and Ordovician paleopoles plot in the present Atlantic Ocean, which is consistent with previously reported paleomagnetic poles. A newly constructed APWP between the Cambrian and Ordovician indicates that the NCB was located in the Southern Hemisphere around 15ëS during Cambro±Ordovician time. Motion of the NCB between the Early and Middle Cambrian comprised: a counterclockwise rotation of 22.3ë  7.0ë and a northward latitudinal displacement of 7.2ë  6.8ë. The Clearwater anorthosite offers the pos- sibility of a pre-2.1 Ga age because it appears in- terlayered and folded with Archean gneisses of the Western Granulite Domain and may have been up- lifted before 2.1 Ga. If the Superior and Rae=Hearne provinces contain magmatic products related to the opening of the Manikewan ocean, then prior to 2.1 Ga they may have been joined. In this paper we test this idea through the use of paleomagnetism, anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and Ar±Ar geochronology, by searching for a possible pre-2.1 Ga uplift-related remanence that might be compared to well-dated magnetizations in the Su- perior Province such as those from the 2167 Ma Biscotasing and 2216 Ma Seneterre dyke swarms (Buchan et al., 1993). 2. Geology The Clearwater complex comprises a layered cumulate sequence dominated by anorthosite and anorthositic norite to gabbro (Scott, 1985; Hulbert, 1988). The rocks are often extremely fresh with primary calcic plagioclase, clinopyroxene, orthopy- roxene and olivine. The complex exhibits primary layering, which dips on average about 35ëSE and is normally expressed by

egmatite dykes and granitic sheets locally cut the anorthosite and may be related to this event (Crocker et al., 1993). 3. Methodology 3.1. Paleomagnetism About 120 samples, each oriented using both magnetic and sun compasses, were ®eld-drilled at 13 sites mainly in anorthosite, along a 7.5 km long traverse oriented normal to strike (Fig. 3). The samples were subject to alternating ®eld (AF) and thermal demagnetization using Schonstedt de- magnetizer models GSD-1 and TSD-1, respectively. Therefore the issue remains as to what proportion of the arcuate fea- tures are secondary, and what proportion are primary. To address this problem, we conducted a palaeo- magnetic investigation of the Mweelrea Ignimbrites (Llanvirn), in the South Mayo Trough (SMT) which lies to the north of our previous studies in the Sil- urian of north Galway. The palaeomagnetism of the Mweelrea Ignimbrites has been studied by Deutsch and Somayajulu (1969) and Morris (1973). Although both studies yielded qualitative evidence for a pri- mary magnetic remanence approximately concor- dant with that expected for Laurentia (Briden et al., 1989), the results are based on limited demagneti- sation procedures and have large error margins. The Deutsch and Somayajulu (1969) study, in particular, was also characterised by a rather limited geographi- cal coverage of sampling sites. Neither of the earlier palaeomagnetic studies addressed the possibility of within-terrane relative rotation. 34 C. Mac Niocaill et al. / Tectonophysics 299 (1998) 31±47 2. Geological setting and sampling In this paper we follow the time scale of Tucker and McKerrow (1995) in describing series names, with the exception of the Llanv

Tucker and McKerrow (1995) in describing series names, with the exception of the Llanvirn series, which now includes the Llandeilo as a stage (Fortey et al., 1995). In this scheme the Early Ordovician comprises the Tremadoc and Arenig (495±480 and 480±470 Ma, respectively), the middle Ordovician consists of the Llanvirn series (470±458 Ma) and the Late Ordovi- cian comprises the Caradoc and Ashgill (458±449 and 449±443 Ma, respectively). The Silurian is sub- divided into four series: the Llandovery (443±428 Ma), the Wenlock (428±423 Ma), the Ludlow (423± 419 Ma) and the Pridoli (419±417 Ma). The Mweelrea Ignimbrites form part of the Mweelrea Formation, a 2-km (minimum)-thick se- quence of coarse-grained, trough cross-bedded sand- stones with local conglomerates and slates exposed in the SMT. The sands contain volcanic, granitic, and continental metamorphic detritus. Abdeldayem 1 Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Tanta Uni˝ersity, Tanta, Egypt Received 22 September 1998; accepted 25 September 1998 Abstract The palaeomagnetic and rock magnetic characteristics of some Cenozoic rocks from the Cairo±Fayum area have been .investigated. A total number of 259 oriented core samples were collected at 32 sites located in rocks of Eocene 13 sites , .  .Oligocene 11 sites and Pliocene 9 sites ages. Most of these rocks carry a weak but stable remanent magnetisation that is principally carried by hematite. Goethite and magnetite are also found in some samples as subordinate constituents. Careful thermal demagnetisation successfully enabled the isolation of the characteristic remanent magnetisation. Normal and reversed polarities that passed a reversal test have been recorded in the three age groups. This magnetisation is probably of primary origin and reflects the ages of the rocks. Palaeomagnetic measurements In the present study new palaeomagnetic results from Tertiary volcanic occurrences of the Siebenge- birge and the Westerwald are presented. These vol- canic ®elds are located at the northeastern part of the Rhenish Massif (Fig. 12). The new palaeomagnetic results are compared with (1) the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of Tertiary central Europe and Ð giving even more evidence Ð (2) with palaeo- magnetic results of the neighbouring volcanic areas Hocheifel, V ogelsberg and RhoÈn, which were active at about the same time period. Older palaeomag- netic results from Siebengebirge and Westerwald derived from Nairn and Ku Èrsten (1959) and Nairn (1962) did not seem to be very reliable because of missing detailed demagnetization experiments and corresponding analyses of remanent magnetization. Here we present the results of our new palaeomag- netic investigations of 36 sites of the Westerwald and 19 sites of the Siebengebirge Tertiary volcanic ®elds (Rotsch, 1997; Fig. 1, Table 1). 2.1. Based on the magnetic anomaly lineations, Isezaki (1986) pro- posed that the opening started at 19 Ma and ceased at 15 Ma in the Japan Basin when the half spreading rate was assumed to be 3.4 cm =year. Kono (1986) found that a typical wavelength of 30 to 50 km in the eastern part of the East Sea represents a ¯uctuation of Miocene geomagnetic reversal polarity of 0.3± 0.5 Ma scale when the spreading rate was assumed as about 10 cm =year. He pointed out that the dif®- culty of identifying the magnetic pro®le in the East Sea because of the possibilities of spreading from multiple ridges or frequent ridge jumps, a distorted skewness by later thermal events or block motion in the crust, and a deep or thin magnetic source layer. He proposed a one-sided spreading model for the East Sea opening during Anomalies 5B (15 Ma) to 5AA (13 Ma) with a ridge jump at 5AC (14 Ma). 6. The sinistral Tsushima±Goto tectonic line is the most probable tectonic boundary in the west of SW Japan (Ishikawa et al., 1989). This idea is strongly sup- ported by the considerable counterclockwise block rotations around 15 Ma based on paleomagnetic data from the Tsushima and Goto Islands (Ishikawa and Tagami, 1991) and the existence of compressive de- formation and thrust belts, 100 km wide (Fig. 9c), about northwestern SW Japan. 10. Conclusions Dual polarity paleomagnetic data obtained from Tertiary rocks in the southeastern Korean Peninsula indicate a close relationship with the opening of the East Sea. A large clockwise block rotation by dextral move- ment of the Yangsan Fault on the Korean Peninsula occurred at 17.3 Ma, and is interpreted as revealing a parallel spreading event before a fan-shaped rota- tional event of the Japanese Islands (at around 15 Ma) during the opening of the East Sea. Much more paleomagnetic data (for example, for Cenozoic rocks in the Yeonil Basin) is needed to clarify rotational time, tectonic process and mecha- nism of the Pohang area. In this study, paleomag- netic results are presented for the Tertiary volcanic and sedimentary rocks from both the Yeonil and Yangnam Basins in the southern part of the Ko- rean Peninsula in order to obtain more informations about the time of the clockwise rotation event of the area. We also obtained new paleomagnetic data for the Eocene V olcanic Rocks in the Yeonil Basin offering more concrete tectonic scheme of the area. The analysis of the results combined with previous data suggests a probable model of opening of the East Sea, which is interpreted as correlating with northward migration of the Philippine Sea Plate. 2. Geologic setting In the Korean Peninsula, several Tertiary basins exist along the coast of the East Sea (Neogene and Paleogene) and the west coast region (Paleogene) of the Peninsula (Fig. 1). The sinistral Tsushima±Goto tectonic line is the most probable tectonic boundary in the west of SW Japan (Ishikawa et al., 1989). This idea is strongly sup- ported by the considerable counterclockwise block rotations around 15 Ma based on paleomagnetic data from the Tsushima and Goto Islands (Ishikawa and Tagami, 1991) and the existence of compressive de- formation and thrust belts, 100 km wide (Fig. 9c), about northwestern SW Japan. 10. A large clockwise block rotation by dextral move- ment of the Yangsan Fault on the Korean Peninsula occurred at 17.3 Ma, and is interpreted as revealing a parallel spreading event before a fan-shaped rota- tional event of the Japanese Islands (at around 15 Ma) during the opening of the East Sea. In this study, paleomag- netic results are presented for the Tertiary volcanic and sedimentary rocks from both the Yeonil and Yangnam Basins in the southern part of the Ko- rean Peninsula in order to obtain more informations about the time of the clockwise rotation event of the area. ted 30 October 1998 Abstract Two different distributions of declinations with dual polarities are found in the Tertiary rocks of the Yeonil Basin and Yangnam Basin along the Yangsan Fault in the southeastern part of the Korean Peninsula. These are northward declinations in the Middle Miocene Yeonil Group and strong eastward declinations in the Early Miocene Yangbuk Group and in the Eocene V olcanic Rocks. This is interpreted by invoking (1) the Yangsan Fault as a dextral wrench fault system by spreading in the Uleung Basin of the East Sea (Sea of Japan), and (2) a clockwise vertical rotation caused by the movement of the fault at around 17.3 Ma just prior to the sedimentation of the Yeonil Group. target_context.excerpt: act Two different distributions of declinations with dual polarities are found in the Tertiary rocks of the Yeonil Basin and Yangnam Basin along the Yangsan Fault in the southeastern part of the Korean Peninsula. These are northward declinations in the Middle Miocene Yeonil Group and strong eastward declinations in the Early Miocene Yangbuk Group and in the Eocene V olcanic Rocks. This is interpreted by invoking (1) the Yangsan Fault as a dextral wrench fault system by spreading in the Uleung Basin of the East Sea (Sea of Japan), and (2) a clockwise vertical rotation caused by the movement of the fault at around 17.3 Ma just prior to the sedimentation of the Yeonil Group. The Gingenbullen Dolerite (GB) (34.5°S, 150.3°E) and the Gibraltar Microsyenite (GS) (34.5°S, 150.4°E) were emplaced during the second of three major phases of igneous activity that aVected the southern Sydney Basin and are K/Ar dated at 172 and 178 Ma, respectively. The magnetic mineralogy of the two intrusions is diVerent: the GB is dominated by single-domain (SD)/pseudo-single-domain grains of magnetite, whereas the GS has both SD magnetite and haematite components, although the haematite component does not record a stable remanence. The GB records two opposed components of magnetization, above 100 °C, occupying distinct parts of the blocking temperature spectrum. The lower blocking temperature (LBT) component resides between 150 and 400 °C and is of normal polarity, having a mean direction of D/I=021°/−79° (a95=8°, k=63), with a corresponding VGP at Lat/Long = 54°S/137°E( dp=12, dm=13). This component is believed to be a TCRM or TVRM related to the initial opening of the Tasman Sea at ~90 Ma. T

They date from around 197 Ma and the flows are mainly tholeiitic basalts with a low TiO 2 and incompatible element content. The magnetic carriers in rocks from these two formations were highly oxidized titanomagnetites, maghemites and, probably, titanomaghemites. Paleomagnetic analysis has shown that the magneti- zations are all normal in polarity and virtual geomagnetic poles obtained for both formations are indistinguishable at the 95% confidence level. The calculated mean for these poles is 250.3°E, 65.5°S (N = 15; A95 = 3.6°; Ksc = 1578). This pole is compatible with Jurassic poles which have been determined for South America or transposed from Africa. 1. Introduction The tectonomagmatic reactivation of the South American Platform since the Permo-Triassic is related to the fragmentation of Gondwana and to the opening of the Atlantic Ocean. Ma

m. Samples for this study came from the basalt formations of Anari in the State of Rondonia and Tapirapufi in the State of Mato Grosso. The motivation for the selection of these two formations was the scarce data on their pale- omagnetism, geochronology and geochemistry, which made it impossible to conclude whether such basalts could belong to the flood tholeiites of the Early Cretaceous Serra Geral Formation (Paranfi Basin), with which the basalts had previ- ously been associated ([8], and references therein). The intermediate component (B) was generally separated between 200 ° C and 660 ° C. section_candidates.excerpt: ed three components of magnetization. The most unstable component (A) was removed between 200 ° C and 500 ° C, which corresponds to the local present ﬁeld direction. The intermediate component (B) was generally separated between 200 ° C and 660 ° C. The omnipresence of this complex secondary component across the Northern Suture Zone suggests that movement of chemically active orogenic ﬂuids at, or slightly before, the time of the India–Asia collision was probably responsible for the authigenic remagnetization processes. The characteristic component (C) was generally unblocked between 600 ° C and 685 ° C. The characteristic directions from 12 sites fall into two groups. The sites from the Purit Formation give a tilt-corrected mean direction of D=311.2° , I=–4.4° , k=12.4, a95=17.8° , indicating a counter-clockwise rotation of about 66 ° and 15° relative to Eurasia and India, respectively. The tilt-corrected mean direction for the Reshun and Drosh formations is D=263.0° , I=2.2° , k=52.7, a95=10.6° , which indicates that the sampling area experienced a counter-clockwise rotation of about 114 ° and 63° with respect to Eurasia and India, respectively. In both cases the palaeomagnetic rotation is consistent with the regional superstructure of the Hindukush–Pamir–Karakoram syntaxial bend.

carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: ediments rapidly deposited in a rift which developed within an Andean-type batholith in juxtaposition to the southern margin of the Laurentian Shield in South Greenland atca. 1300 Ma. The lavas have been shown to preserve a detailed record of the geomagnetic ﬁeld at the time of eruption, incorporating normal, reversed and transitional directions. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) studies are amongst the most sensitive for detecting trace concentrations of magnetic minerals (Robertson & France 1994) and have been applied in this study to highlight types and relative amounts of magnetic minerals. Selected samples were magnetized using a pulse magnetizer, and applied ﬁelds were increased in approximately logarithmic steps (2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 80, 100, 120, 120, 160, 200, 250, 300 mT …) until an upper limit of 2500 mT was reached. Although the peak ﬁeld in the pulse demagnetizer is unable to fully saturate minerals with high coercivities such as haematite, it is adequate to identify the essential behaviour of this mineral. Subsequently, samples were incrementally magnetized by the same process in the opposing direction until the IRMs were reduced to zero. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) studies are amongst the most sensitive for detecting trace concentrations of magnetic minerals (Robertson & France 1994) and have been applied in this study to highlight types and relative amounts of magnetic minerals. Selected samples were magnetized using a pulse magnetizer, and applied ﬁelds were increased in approximately logarithmic steps (2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 80, 100, 120, 120, 160, 200, 250, 300 mT …) until an upper limit of 2500 mT was reached. Although the peak ﬁeld in the pulse demagnetizer is unable to fully saturate minerals with high coercivities such as haematite, it is adequate to identify the essential behaviour of this mineral. Subsequently, samples were incrementally magnetized by the same process in the opposing direction until the IRMs were reduced to zero. At this point the applied ﬁeld value deﬁnes the coercivity of the sample remanence (Hcr). IRM acquisition curves (Fig. 7) are similar but indicate signiﬁcantly higher coercivities in samples from the Mussartuˆt and Naujurssuit formations compared to results from the Maˆjuˆt Formation.
